title: My dad called every Sunday at six
lesson: If someone keeps calling you about nothing, it's never about nothing. It's them saying they love you. So pick up. Or better, call them first.

beats.vo: For two years, my dad called me every Sunday at six. And for two years, I mostly let it ring.
beats.shot: Her small London flat kitchen: white metro tiles, a pale wood worktop, a small white two-ring hob, a white sash window with November rain running down the glass onto wet grey slate rooftops. Close-up on the pale wood worktop: a black phone lies face down beside a cream ceramic mixing bowl, buzzing and shuffling a little on the wood. Her hand (slender young hands, short natural pale-pink nails, no rings) in an oversized oatmeal hoodie sleeve rests on the worktop beside it, still, then slowly draws back out of the frame. In real time. The sharp buzz of a phone against the wood, rain on the window.

beats.vo: It's Sunday. Ten to six. I'm making his stew. And I want to tell you why I never miss that call now.

beats.vo: My dad's not a talker. Ask how he is, he says fine. Ask about the weather, you get twenty minutes.
beats.shot: Soft bright grey November daylight. Her dad's small back garden: a small glass greenhouse with tall tomato plants tied to canes, a dry-stone wall, a wet grey stone patio with three stone steps, green fells and low grey cloud beyond. Dad (short neat grey hair receding a little at the temples, a short trimmed grey beard, thin silver wire-framed glasses, kind light-blue eyes), in a navy wool crew-neck jumper over a light-blue collared shirt, stands still on the stone patio beside the greenhouse, hands in his trouser pockets, seen from the side, looks up slowly at the low grey cloud over the fells, then gives a small thoughtful nod to himself. beats.vo: After a while, I stopped picking up at all. I'd watch his name light up and think, next week.
beats.shot: Evening, one plain lamp. In real time. A muffled buzz on fabric, rain on a window.

beats.vo: He never complained. He'd just leave a short message. Hi love. Just me. Nothing important.

beats.shot: Evening, soft fading blue daylight. A white sash window of a small London flat, rain running down the glass, wet grey slate rooftops and chimney pots beyond, two small pots of herbs on the sill, no person. In real time. Rain on glass.

beats.vo: Then one Sunday in November, six o'clock came. And my phone didn't ring.
beats.shot: Evening, soft fading blue daylight at the window and one plain ceiling lamp on. beats.vo: Finally, his neighbour picked up. Dad had slipped on the wet steps that morning.
beats.shot: Dusk, soft grey light, rain falling. Her dad's small back garden: three wet grey stone patio steps glistening with rain, a green garden glove lying on the bottom step, the greenhouse and dry-stone wall behind, no person. In real time. Steady rain on stone.

beats.vo: He was okay. A broken wrist and a bruised pride. But he'd sat in A and E all afternoon, alone.

beats.vo: Tomatoes did well. Pepper's hip is better. Ask about her job.
beats.shot: Evening, soft fading blue daylight at the small window and one plain ceiling lamp on. beats.vo: And at the bottom: Tell her I'm proud of her. That line had been there for months. He never got to say it, because I never picked up.

beats.vo: I stood by the kettle and cried. Quietly, so he wouldn't hear.
beats.shot: Evening, soft fading blue daylight at the small window and one plain ceiling lamp on. Ellie, her chestnut braid over her left shoulder, in a cream wool roll-neck jumper, seen from behind at the deep white stone sink, both hands resting on its edge, shoulders lowered, a steel kettle steaming softly beside her, perfectly still and calm. In real time. A kettle starting to boil, rain on the small window.

beats.vo: Those calls were never about tomatoes. That was him saying, I miss you, the only way he knew.
beats.shot: Evening, soft fading blue daylight at the small window and one plain ceiling lamp on. beats.vo: I stayed the week. He couldn't cook with one hand, so I made his beef stew. The one he made every Sunday when I was little.
beats.shot: Soft bright grey November daylight from the small window. Her dad's small old stone cottage kitchen in the Yorkshire Dales: dark wooden beams, cream painted walls, an old cream enamel range cooker, a scrubbed pine table, a cream corded telephone on the wall by the back door. Ellie (long chestnut-brown hair in a loose low braid over her left shoulder, light freckles across the nose and cheeks, light-hazel eyes), in a navy-and-white striped Breton long-sleeve top, stands at the old cream range seen from the side, head bowed, eyes on a dark-red cast-iron pot of dark-brown beef stew with orange carrot chunks, slowly stirring with a wooden spoon, steam rising. Ordinary everyday movement at real-life speed, a small pause, one small head movement at most, the face stays the same; the camera stays locked off, it does not follow anyone. The soft bubble of stew, a spoon on cast iron.

beats.vo: He sat at the table and gave orders. More carrots. No, more than that.
beats.shot: Soft bright grey November daylight from the small window. Her dad's small old stone cottage kitchen in the Yorkshire Dales: dark wooden beams, cream painted walls, an old cream enamel range cooker, a scrubbed pine table, a cream corded telephone on the wall by the back door. Over Ellie's shoulder (her chestnut braid and striped Breton top soft in the foreground at the range): Dad (short neat grey hair receding a little at the temples, a short trimmed grey beard, thin silver wire-framed glasses, kind light-blue eyes), in a dark-green wool crew-neck jumper, his right forearm in a navy-blue arm sling with a white cast on the wrist, sits at the pine table looking at her, says something short and dry, and nods once at the pot with a small dry smile. Only his mouth moves, softly, no words heard. Ordinary everyday movement at real-life speed, a small pause, one small head movement at most, the face stays the same; the camera stays locked off, it does not follow anyone. The soft room, the stew bubbling.

beats.vo: So, more carrots. And he was right. He's always annoyingly right about stew.
beats.shot: Soft bright grey November daylight from the small window. Her dad's small old stone cottage kitchen in the Yorkshire Dales: dark wooden beams, cream painted walls, an old cream enamel range cooker, a scrubbed pine table, a cream corded telephone on the wall by the back door. Close-up over a cream ceramic bowl: her hands (slender young hands, short natural pale-pink nails, no rings) in navy-and-white striped sleeves peel a long orange carrot with a plain vegetable peeler, orange peel ribbons falling into the bowl beside two peeled carrots. In real time. The crisp scrape of a peeler on a carrot.

beats.vo: We talked more that week than in the two years before.

beats.vo: Now it's Sunday again. The stew's nearly ready.
beats.shot: Evening, soft fading blue daylight at the window and one plain ceiling lamp on. Her small London flat kitchen: white metro tiles, a pale wood worktop, a small white two-ring hob, a white sash window with November rain running down the glass onto wet grey slate rooftops. Close-up: a dark-red cast-iron pot with its lid already off, standing on the small white hob, full of dark-brown beef stew with orange carrot chunks, softly bubbling, a thin wisp of steam rising. No hands, no person, nothing else moves. A completely still locked-off frame: the camera never moves, every edge of the window and tiles stays in the same place from the first frame to the last. In real time. The soft bubble of stew, rain on the window.

beats.vo: His wrist healed fine. Pepper's still slow. The tomatoes are done for the year. I know all that, because I listen now.
beats.shot: Evening, soft fading blue daylight at the window and one plain ceiling lamp on. Ellie (long chestnut-brown hair in a loose low braid over her left shoulder, light freckles across the nose and cheeks, light-hazel eyes), in a sage-green cotton jumper with the sleeves pushed to the forearm, stands at the worktop seen from the side and sets a black phone face up on the pale wood next to the hob, its dark screen plain, then rests her hand beside it, eyes on it. Ordinary everyday movement at real-life speed, a small pause, one small head movement at most, the face stays the same; the camera stays locked off, it does not follow anyone. A phone set down against wood, the stew bubbling, rain.

beats.vo: If someone keeps calling you about nothing, it's never about nothing. It's them saying they love you.
beats.shot: Evening, soft fading blue daylight at the small window and one plain ceiling lamp on. Her dad's small old stone cottage kitchen in the Yorkshire Dales: dark wooden beams, cream painted walls, an old cream enamel range cooker, a scrubbed pine table, a cream corded telephone on the wall by the back door. Dad (short neat grey hair receding a little at the temples, a short trimmed grey beard, thin silver wire-framed glasses, kind light-blue eyes), in an olive quilted gilet over a red-and-navy checked flannel shirt, sits on a wooden chair by the cream range, the cream wall phone's receiver at his ear, the curly cord hanging, Pepper, the old black-and-white border collie (grey muzzle, narrow white blaze, white chest and paws, her left ear folded over) lying at his feet; he listens, and a small slow smile comes. Ordinary everyday movement at real-life speed, a small pause, one small head movement at most, the face stays the same; the camera stays locked off, it does not follow anyone. beats.shot: Evening, soft fading blue light. A white sash window of a small London flat, rain running down the glass, wet slate rooftops beyond and one warm lit window across the street, two small pots of herbs on the sill, no person.
